screens.title: State Variables and Storage
screens.subtitle: Where data lives, why it costs gas, and how to avoid costly mistakes

narration.text: In this lesson we will build a clear mental model of where data lives in Solidity and why that matters for correctness and gas cost. Solidity has three explicit data locations — persistent storage, ephemeral memory, and read-only calldata. Storage is the chain's persistent ledger; memory is temporary working space during a transaction; calldata is a read-only envelope for external inputs. You will see how state variables map to storage slots, how function parameters can be memory or calldata, and how constant and immutable keywords let you avoid storage reads. I will also show practical examples where a careless assignment makes a full copy of a large array and dramatically increases gas. By the end you will be able to choose the correct data location for a function parameter, reason about when assignments create references versus copies, and use immutable or constant to optimize hot reads. Consider a user profile mapping: choosing a storage reference instead of copying to memory saves gas and avoids bugs. Are you ready to see specific patterns and a small refactor that makes a function far cheaper?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Storage = persistent & expensive; memory = temporary & cheaper; calldata = read-only and most efficient for external input. Use constant/immutable to reduce storage reads.

screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives guide practice and assessment. First, you will distinguish storage, memory, and calldata: know their persistence, mutability, and gas profile. That means you should be able to explain why an external function benefits from calldata for a large array. Second, you will declare, initialize, and reason about state variables so that you safely persist values on-chain and understand the cost of each write. Third, you will compare gas costs of storage reads and writes versus memory and calldata, and use that comparison to optimize code paths. Fourth, you will use constant and immutable appropriately: constants for compile-time values embedded into bytecode, immutables for deployment-time values set in the constructor, and regular storage for mutable data. Each objective includes a short practice prompt and a verification milestone where you refactor a small contract. These skills are practical: they reduce operational cost and eliminate subtle bugs caused by unintended copies. Ready to proceed with step-by-step examples and a refactor challenge?

screens.title: What is storage?
screens.subtitle: Persistent state variables and their gas characteristics

narration.text: Storage in Solidity is the persistent region where contract-level variables live. When you declare a state variable outside any function, such as an unsigned integer counter or a mapping of addresses to balances, the value is written into storage slots on the blockchain. This persistence is what makes contracts useful across transactions, but it also introduces cost: reading from storage consumes gas, and writing to storage is significantly more expensive because it modifies the global state. For example, incrementing a stored counter will cost gas proportional to the storage write. A practical pattern is to minimize writes — compute values in memory first and write a single updated value back to storage. Another important point is reference semantics: when you get a struct from a mapping using a storage qualifier, you modify the original data in place rather than creating a copy. A common misconception is to treat storage like cheap R A M; it is not. Think of storage as a shared hard drive: persistent, replicated, and costly to change. Can you spot places where a single write can replace multiple writes and lower gas?

keyIdea.title: Storage summary
keyIdea.text: State variables live in storage, persistence across transactions incurs the highest gas cost, and storage references modify data in place.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › What is storage?
Definition
Persistent contract-level storage that survives transactions and function calls.
Characteristics
  • Persistent across transactions and calls.
  • Expensive to write; reads cost gas too.
  • Reference semantics when using storage qualifiers.
Misconception
Treating storage as cheap temporary space leads to expensive and slow contracts.
Key Takeaway

Minimize storage writes. Use storage references to update in place rather than copying and rewriting full structs or arrays.

Concrete example
Mapping of users with a storage reference for deactivation.
// Access and modify a storage struct by reference
User storage userToDeactivate = users[_userAddress];
userToDeactivate.active = false; // modifies storage in-place
Why it matters
Updating via a storage reference avoids copying a struct into memory and reassigning it, saving gas and preventing accidental mismatches between copies.
Common mistake
Copying large arrays from storage to memory when unnecessary. This creates an expensive deep copy.

narration.text: Memory is the temporary workspace Solidity uses during a function call. Variables declared inside functions or parameters of complex types default to memory unless explicitly given another qualifier. Memory lives only for the duration of the call and is cleared afterward. Because it is ephemeral and less expensive than storage, memory is ideal for intermediate calculations, sorting, or building temporary arrays before committing a single result to storage. Remember that assigning a storage variable to a memory variable creates a copy. That copy is independent; modifying it will not change the original storage. A subtle point is when you pass arrays to internal functions: if you do not mark the parameter as storage, you may copy the array into memory implicitly, which can be costly for large arrays. A practical rule is to use memory for local processing and only write back to storage once. A common misconception is assuming memory is free — it’s cheaper than storage but still consumes gas for large allocations. How can you restructure a computation to keep heavy processing in memory before a single storage write?

keyIdea.title: Memory summary
keyIdea.text: Memory is temporary, cheaper than storage, and is used for local variables and intermediate processing. Copies from storage to memory create independent copies.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › What is memory?
Definition & behavior
Ephemeral workspace that lasts only during a function call. Use for temporary arrays, local computation, and function parameters when safe.
Characteristics
  • Cleared at the end of the call.
  • Cheaper than storage for reads/writes, but still costs gas for large allocations.
  • Assigning storage to memory creates a deep copy.
Key Takeaway

Keep heavy computation in memory and avoid needless copies from storage for large collections unless you must persist results.

Concrete example: processing an input array
function processArrayInMemory(uint[] memory _inputArray) public pure returns (uint sum) {
  for (uint i = 0; i < _inputArray.length; i++) {
    sum += _inputArray[i];
  }
}
Misconception
Assuming memory copies are free. If you copy a large storage array into memory, that deep copy is costly.

screens.title: What is calldata?
screens.subtitle: Read-only external arguments and gas efficiency

narration.text: Calldata is a specialized, read-only data location Solidity uses for external function parameters. Data placed in calldata is not copied into memory for external calls; instead the function reads directly from the transaction input, which makes calldata the most gas-efficient option for large read-only arrays or structs. Calldata is immutable inside the function — you cannot modify arguments stored there — which both simplifies reasoning and avoids accidental writes. Use calldata for external functions that only need to read large inputs, for example an external batch-processing function that validates a list of addresses. Public functions behave differently: their parameters are typically copied to memory for internal use, which is less efficient. A common pitfall is forgetting to mark an external parameter as calldata and paying unnecessary gas for the implicit copy. Remember: calldata is the sealed envelope of an external call — efficient and immutable. How would you refactor a public function into an external function using calldata to save gas for large arrays? What is calldata? means calldata is read-only, most gas-efficient for external inputs, and avoids copies to memory for large arguments.. In practical terms, read-only external arguments and gas efficiency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Calldata summary
keyIdea.text: Calldata is read-only, most gas-efficient for external inputs, and avoids copies to memory for large arguments.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › What is calldata?
Definition & behavior
Immutable, read-only region used for external function arguments. Most efficient for large, read-only inputs.
When to use
  • External functions that only read arguments.
  • Large arrays or structs passed from off-chain callers.
  • Batch validation routines where no modification is required.
Key Takeaway

Prefer calldata for large external inputs to avoid copies into memory and reduce gas usage.

Concrete example
// External function using calldata for efficiency
function processExternalArray(uint[] calldata _data) external pure returns (uint product) {
  product = 1;
  for (uint i = 0; i < _data.length; i++) {
    product *= _data[i];
  }
}
Misconception
Declaring a parameter without calldata on an external function may cause an implicit copy to memory, increasing gas cost unexpectedly.

screens.title: Storage vs Memory: copy or reference?
screens.subtitle: How assignments behave and when a copy is made

narration.text: Assignments in Solidity either create references or copies depending on data location and types. When you assign a storage variable to another storage variable, you create a reference: both variables point to the same storage slot. Changing one affects the other and writes to storage. Conversely, assigning a storage array or struct to a memory variable creates a deep copy in memory. That copy is independent and modifying it does not alter storage. This behavior matters for gas and correctness. If you need to update a struct held in a mapping, retrieving it as a storage reference and modifying fields in place is both cheaper and less error-prone than copying it to memory, changing values, and writing back. A common mistake is to assume that assigning to a local variable avoids storage writes — it may in fact cause an unintended deep copy. Consider the provided contract examples: the bad pattern copies a storage array into memory unnecessarily, while the good pattern iterates directly on storage or uses a storage reference. As a takeaway, explicitly specify storage or memory for complex types in parameters and locals so you control whether a copy or reference is created. How would you check your code to ensure you are not making unnecessary copies?

keyIdea.title: Assignment rule
keyIdea.text: storage-to-storage creates a reference; storage-to-memory creates a copy. Be explicit to avoid accidental copies and gas spikes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Copy vs Reference
Bad: Unnecessary copy
function getNumbersSumBad() public view returns (uint) {
  uint[] memory tempNumbers = numbers; // copies storage->memory (expensive)
  uint sum = 0;
  for (uint i = 0; i < tempNumbers.length; i++) {
    sum += tempNumbers[i];
  }
  return sum;
}
This copies the whole array into memory, which may be costly for large arrays and is unnecessary for read-only aggregation.
Good: Iterate storage directly
function getNumbersSumGood() public view returns (uint) {
  uint sum = 0;
  for (uint i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++) {
    sum += numbers[i]; // reads directly from storage slots
  }
  return sum;
}
Iterating the storage array avoids copying and reduces gas when only reading values.
Check your code
  • Search for assignments from storage to memory for large arrays or structs.
  • Prefer storage references when you need to edit mapping entries in place.

screens.title: Constants and immutables
screens.subtitle: When to use constant and immutable for gas savings

narration.text: Solidity provides constant and immutable keywords to avoid storing certain values in storage, which reduces gas on reads. A constant is a compile-time constant embedded into the bytecode. Use constant for values truly known at compile time, like a maximum supply. These values do not occupy storage slots and reading them does not trigger a storage read, making them extremely cheap. An immutable value is slightly different: its value is set once during contract deployment, typically in the constructor, and then cannot change. The runtime assigns that value into the contract's bytecode region rather than a storage slot, so reads are cheaper than regular storage reads. Use immutable for deployment-time values such as the deployer address or a configuration parameter passed at construction. A common misconception is that immutable variables take no gas at all — they are cheaper than storage reads but still cost some gas to access. Use constant when truly compile-time; use immutable when the value depends on constructor inputs. Can you identify variables in your contracts that are constant or immutable candidates? Constants and immutables means use constant for compile-time values and immutable for deployment-time values to avoid storage reads and lower gas.. In practical terms, when to use constant and immutable for gas savings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Constants & Immutables
Constant
Values known at compile time are embedded into bytecode and avoid storage slots.
uint public constant MAX_LIMIT = 1000; // compile-time constant
Immutable
Set once during deployment in the constructor; cheaper than storage for reads.
address public immutable deployer;

constructor() {
  deployer = msg.sender; // set at deployment
}
Key Takeaway

Identify values that never change or change only at deployment and mark them constant/immutable to cut storage reads.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: Patterns that create unnecessary gas costs

narration.text: There are recurring mistakes developers make with data locations that lead to higher gas or bugs. First, copying large storage arrays into memory when only read operations are needed. Avoid this by iterating storage directly or passing calldata for external inputs. Second, failing to mark function parameters explicitly as storage or memory for internal functions, which can trigger implicit expensive copies. Explicit qualifiers clarify intent and control whether you are referencing or copying. Third, updating a mapping entry by building a whole new struct in memory and then assigning it back rather than obtaining a storage reference and modifying fields in place. The latter is both cheaper and clearer. Fourth, using public functions when external suffices, leading to implicit memory copies; prefer external with calldata for large inputs. To avoid these problems, adopt a checklist: mark parameters, prefer calldata for external reads, use storage references for mapping edits, and identify constants and immutables. Practice refactoring a function by replacing memory with calldata and confirm gas reduction with a local test. What checklist item will you apply first in your codebase?

keyIdea.title: Avoid these mistakes
keyIdea.text: Don't copy large arrays from storage to memory, be explicit about qualifiers, prefer calldata for large external inputs, and use storage references to update mapping entries.

screens.title: Gas implications: read vs write
screens.subtitle: Comparing operations across storage, memory, and calldata

narration.text: Gas cost is a central concern when choosing data locations. Broadly, storage writes are the most expensive operation because they modify the blockchain's persistent state. Storage reads are cheaper than writes but still cost more than memory or calldata accesses. Memory operations cost gas proportional to the allocated size; small allocations are inexpensive, but large temporary arrays still add cost. Calldata offers the best cost profile for read-only external inputs because it avoids copying data into memory. Consider a function that takes a sizable array from the caller: making the function external and the parameter calldata will often be measurably cheaper than leaving it public and defaulting to a memory copy. Another comparison: writing a struct field in storage directly via a storage reference is cheaper than constructing a full struct in memory and assigning it back. A useful rule of thumb is to move heavy processing into memory and limit storage writes, and use calldata for large inputs to avoid copies. Which functions in your contracts are best suited for calldata? Gas implications: read vs write means writes to storage are most expensive; reads cost less; memory allocations and calldata reads are cheaper — use calldata for large read-only inputs.. In practical terms, comparing operations across storage, memory, and calldata. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Checklist and testing tips
screens.subtitle: How to validate and measure your data-location choices

narration.text: After refactoring, validating behavior and measuring gas are critical. Start with unit tests that exercise create, update, and read paths while asserting correctness. Use a local test runner or a tool to compare gas before and after the refactor. Specifically, measure gas for creating a profile, updating a profile name, and calling any batch-processing functions. Look for large differences when you switch public arrays to external calldata or when you replace a copy pattern with a storage reference. Also test edge cases like empty arrays and maximum-size arrays to ensure no unexpected memory allocation issues. When reviewing code, add inline comments where assignment semantics are subtle: indicate where a storage reference is intentional or where a copy is acceptable. Finally, include a simple lint or checklist in your PR: mark parameters explicit, prefer calldata for external reads, and flag large storage-to-memory copies. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three compact memory cards to carry forward

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential ideas to remember. First, storage is persistent and expensive: minimize writes and prefer in-place updates via storage references for mappings or structs. Second, memory and calldata are temporary: memory is a modifiable workspace for the duration of a call, while calldata is a read-only, most gas-efficient option for external inputs. Use calldata for large external arrays. Third, constant and immutable provide important gas optimizations: constants are embedded at compile time, and immutables are set at deployment and stored outside standard storage slots. Together these patterns reduce gas and eliminate bugs introduced by unintended copies. Review your functions for implicit copies from storage to memory and prefer explicit qualifiers. Keep testing and measuring after each refactor to confirm savings and correctness. Which of these three concepts will you apply first when you return to your code?

Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › What to Remember
Remove unnecessary copies
Iterate storage or use calldata instead of copying large arrays into memory.
Mark qualifiers explicitly
Make storage/memory/calldata explicit in parameters and locals to avoid surprises.
Use constant & immutable
Promote fixed and deployment-time values out of storage to save gas on reads.
Final takeaway

Small, deliberate choices about data location yield safer contracts and meaningful gas savings. Apply the checklist and measure the impact.
